sentences.text: The legal position on this aspect is very clear to the effect that if a particular fact is not challenged in the cross examination, it is deemed to be proved.
Even otherwise, the defendants have failed to prove as to how and in what capacity they came into the possession of the suit property.
Their reliance on their title documents has already been discarded by this court.

As the burden of proof placed upon a party in civil cases is lighter and a party is only required to prove its case on the preponderance of probabilities, this court is of the opinion that the plaintiff has discharged its burden of proof and proved that it had leased out the suit premises in favour of late husband of defendant no.1.
26.
With respect to the validity of oral lease of immoveable property for a period of 20 years, it is relevant to refer to Section 106 of Transfer of Property Act.

As per Section 106 (1) of the Act, in the absence of a contract or local law or usage to the contrary, a lease of immoveable property for any purpose other than agricultural or manufacturing shall be deemed to be a lease from month to month, terminable, on the part of either lessor or lessee, by 15 days notice.

It has been held in judgment 'Punjab National Bank Vs. Ganga Narain Kapur' AIR 1994 All 221 that the legislature intended that a lease of immoveable property for a period of more than one year should be made by registered deed.

entities.text: Punjab National Bank Vs. Ganga Narain Kapur' AIR 1994 All 221
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: But if a lease of immoveable property for a term of more than one year is not made by registered deed or is made orally then in such cases, the presumption about the duration of lease under Section 106 T.P. Act will apply.
Accordingly, in the present case, the lease in question is deemed to be a lease from month to month basis.

sentences.text: This principle prevents a tenant in occupation of the demised premises, from denying the title of the landlord, who let him into possession.

In Stringer's Estate, LR. Ch. 9, Jessel M.R., explained the spirit and rationale underlying the doctrine of estoppel as under:-
"Where a man having no title obtains possession of land under a demise by a man in possession who assumes to give him a title as tenant, he cannot deny his landlord's title.
This is perfectly intelligible doctrine.

He took possession under a contract to pay rent so long as he held possession under the landlord, and to give it up at the end of the term to the landlord, and having taken it in that way he is not allowed to say that the man whose title he admits and under whose title he took possession has not a title.
That is a well-established doctrine.
That is estoppel by contract."
